result: The flexible β-hairpin arms of Fis dimers contact the DNA binding domain (DBD) of Hin, specifically at helix 1, with key interactions involving Hin residues Arg154 and Leu155. These contacts sandwich the Hin dimers to promote remodeling into the active tetramer.
evaluation: Reviewers explicitly praised the crosslinking experiments as 'clever and comprehensive' and noted that the work 'reveal[s] the important contacts of the Hin invertasome both with Fis and with the enhancer DNA.' The only concern raised (comment 5) about proper folding of mutants K51A and K158A was addressed by the H107Y control experiments shown in Figure 4C, which reviewers acknowledged 'appears to be taken care of.'

result: A basic region on the Hin catalytic domain (helix-B region, residues 47-51) contacts enhancer DNA between the Fis binding sites to complete assembly of the active Hin tetramer. Mutations in this region (R47A, R48A, K51A) reduce Fis-activated inversion rates and destabilize the enhancer interaction, leading to increased knotted products.
evaluation: Reviewers found the explanation 'reasonable' but expressed uncertainty about the mechanism, stating 'one can't help but think that perhaps something else is going on as well' (comment 1). They questioned why loss of these interactions leads to multiple rotations and knotted products, suggesting alternative explanations involving product DNA interactions. Reviewers requested clarification of the topology experiments and noted the control showing loop size dependence was 'very satisfying,' but the underlying mechanism remains incompletely explained.

result: Fis contacts the DBDs of only the bottom two Hin subunits (bound to hix1L and hix2R) within the cleaved invertasome, with no crosslinks forming at hix1R or hix2L.
evaluation: Reviewers did not raise concerns about the site-specific crosslinking data demonstrating asymmetric Fis-Hin contacts. The experiments were described as part of the 'clever and comprehensive set of experiments' and the model was noted to provide 'a satisfying explanation for how Fis stimulates inversion.'

result: Hin dimers covalently crosslinked to Fis can be remodeled into catalytically-active tetramers competent for DNA cleavage and ligation, demonstrating that the invertasome remains intact throughout the entire reaction.
evaluation: Reviewers did not question these findings. The experiments demonstrating that crosslinked Fis-Hin complexes can complete the reaction were part of the 'clever and comprehensive set of experiments' that reviewers praised. These results support the model that the enhancer remains associated with Hin throughout the reaction.

result: Hin DBD helix 1 residues Q151, R154, and L155 are critical for Fis-activated DNA inversion, with L155A showing >50-fold reduction in inversion rates. However, these mutations do not affect Fis-independent recombination by hyperactive Hin-H107Y mutants.
evaluation: Reviewers praised the experiments in Figure 4C showing that 'helix B mutations are only needed if Fis is' as 'nice experiments' (comment 2). However, they suggested the paper would be 'more interesting if it included some comparison with Rowland et al.'s quite similar experiments on Sin,' indicating the findings are solid but could be better contextualized.

result: The helix-B region and adjacent residues involved in Fis/enhancer contacts in Hin invertases are conserved among DNA invertases but differ in resolvases (Sin, γδ/Tn3), where analogous regions mediate protein-protein contacts during synaptic complex assembly. This suggests a common regulatory mechanism across serine recombinase subfamilies.
evaluation: Reviewers identified this as 'one of the most interesting findings' but noted it 'could be highlighted more clearly in the manuscript' (opening paragraph). They challenged the claim about sequence conservation, stating 'the number of K and R near the end of helix B doesn't look significantly different in the invertases vs resolvases' (comment 3). Reviewers requested better discussion of the 2-3' γδ mutants and Sin mutants with analogous phenotypes (comment 4), and asked whether these contacts merely stabilize complexes or actively promote dimer-to-tetramer remodeling.

result: A structural model of the Fis-bound enhancer shows an S-shaped DNA structure, and the primary Fis-Hin interaction surface involves Val16/Val22 on Fis with Leu155 on Hin, and Asp20 on Fis with Arg154 on Hin.
evaluation: Reviewers did not challenge the structural model or the proposed interaction surfaces. However, they noted presentation issues, stating 'it is sometimes hard to follow where some of the features, helix B etc. that are being discussed in various figures were positioned relative to the tetramer' (comment 6), suggesting better labeling and orientation guides would help readers unfamiliar with the system.

result: The invertasome restricts subunit rotation to a single 180° step when the enhancer-hix distance is short due to torsional strain in the small DNA loop. Multiple connections between Hin tetramer and Fis/enhancer stabilize the complex and restrict processive exchanges.
evaluation: Reviewers found the topological explanation plausible and noted 'the control experiment showing that loop size matters for the WT but not for the mutant is very satisfying' (comment 1). However, they requested clarification of the explanation, asking whether 'with the small loop, if the enhancer stays put, multiple rounds of recombination are energetically uphill because of the conformational strain they'd introduce in the dinky loop.'

result: Background claims describing the Hin/Fis system, serine recombinase mechanisms, invertasome structure and function, and the role of DNA supercoiling in promoting synapsis.
evaluation: These are established background claims supported by citations to previous literature. Reviewers did not question these foundational aspects of the system, treating them as accepted knowledge that provides context for the new findings.
